transcript:
Meeting header: 2027-01-14 16:00 UTC | Duration 41 minutes
Attendees: Nina Patel (Redwood AE), Carlos Romero (Redwood SE), Leah Kim (CTO, Verdigris), Marco Alvarez (Eng Lead), Sofia Li (Product)

[00:00] Nina Patel: Hey everyone thanks for making time, this is Nina from Redwood, uh Carlos is with me our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:06] Leah Kim: Good, thanks. It's 8am for us so caffeinated, Marco and Sofia here.
[00:10] Marco Alvarez: Morning, yep.
[00:12] Carlos Romero: Great to meet you all. Quick agenda — open Qs on quickstart, show time-to-first-token path, and then qualification: usage patterns, security needs, timeline.

[00:30] Sofia Li: Perfect. We're a small startup building a recommendation overlay for e-commerce — we're trying to move from prototype to a PLG onramp so ideally a self-serve flow.
[00:38] Nina Patel: Awesome. Is the plan to let customers sign up and hit the API directly or will you route through your backend?
[00:42] Leah Kim: Initially through backend, server-side calls. We might expose some client features later.
[00:47] Marco Alvarez: Our stack today is Node services in GCP, infra's managed, we use BigQuery for analytics, and we do some caching at the app layer — memcached. Not running Kubernetes yet for inference.

[01:05] Carlos Romero: Got it. For time-to-first-token, our hosted API is usually fastest: sign up, redeem credits, call the REST endpoint or SDK. Typical dev loop — npm install redwood, a couple lines of code or curl — you're generating in minutes.
[01:20] Sofia Li: How quick is quick? Like 5 minutes? 30?
[01:24] Carlos Romero: Realistically 10-20 minutes for a developer to be able to send a token and see a response. If you want to wire SSO + SAML for enterprise flows that'll add time, but for your PLG pilot it's mostly sign up + API key.

[01:40] Leah Kim: We care about cost. Our CFO is sensitive to token cost. What's the delta between hosted and running something ourselves?
[01:48] Nina Patel: Hosted gives you the easiest path — pay per token, no infra ops. If you ran in-house you'd trade that for infra costs, ops, and probably higher engineering time. Dedicated (reserved) comes in when you need predictable throughput and lower per-token price at commit.
[02:05] Marco Alvarez: At what volume does Dedicated make sense?
[02:07] Carlos Romero: It depends on throughput patterns — once you're sustaining a few hundred tokens/sec or need consistent P95s under 200ms for production traffic, Dedicated often becomes more economical. But for a PLG pilot with bursty traffic, hosted + caching is common.

[02:26] Sofia Li: What about Private — we have a few banking clients who might later ask for VPC/on-prem. Is that a long migration?
[02:33] Nina Patel: Private is available; migration path exists but it's a different engagement — enterprise licensing, on-prem packages, and a security review. Usually after you've proved the model with hosted and want to bind to strict data residency.

[02:50] Marco Alvarez: Security — we need SOC2, SSO, audit logs, and probably a KMS. Do you have those?
[02:56] Carlos Romero: Yes. SOC2 Type II is available, SSO/SAML and RBAC are supported, and we integrate with KMS for customer-managed keys in Private. For hosted we offer envelope encryption and managed keys, and we can discuss stricter KMS options for Dedicated/Private.

[03:14] Leah Kim: Any audit log samples?
[03:16] Nina Patel: I'll link the security pack after this call — it's the standard deck plus a sample audit log extract. Link: https://redwood.example.com/security-pack (note: this is the recording link we share)

[03:28] Sofia Li: When you say "redeem credits" how does that actually work? Is there an admin flow?
[03:32] Nina Patel: We send a promo token for your account, you redeem in the console, credits show up. For PLG you can also mint invite codes for customers. For quickstart I'll send step-by-step.

[03:45] Marco Alvarez: For benchmarking, what should we measure? P95, cost per 1k tokens?
[03:50] Carlos Romero: P95 latency, cold start (first request), token cost at 1k/10k/100k scales, and error rate under concurrency. We'll give a small harness — a curl loop or Python script to run from your env.

[04:05] Leah Kim: Can you do a short demo call showing the SDK and a curl example?
[04:08] Carlos Romero: Sure — quick demo now? Or I can drop snippets. We have a tiny example: curl -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate -H "Authorization: Bearer <KEY>" -d '{"prompt":"Hello"}'
[04:24] (small laughter)
[04:26] Carlos Romero: That will give you a synchronous response. For streaming we have a websocket/stream endpoint too. SDKs in Node/Python handle streaming as well.

[04:40] Sofia Li: Any pitfalls with our Node stack? Does the SDK have a small footprint?
[04:44] Carlos Romero: SDK is lightweight, single-dependency. Biggest pitfall is accidentally logging or leaking API keys in client-side code — keep calls server-side. Also watch for default rate limits; we'll show how to increase limits for the pilot.

[05:02] Marco Alvarez: For our use case we expect spikes during sale events, like 10x baseline for short bursts. Will hosted handle that?
[05:08] Nina Patel: Hosted can burst, but if you need strict SLOs during big spikes Dedicated with burst pool or reserved capacity plus autoscaling is a safer choice. We can simulate your spike in a perf test.

[05:28] Sofia Li: Pricing ask — any ballpark for typical startup pilot?
[05:32] Nina Patel: We'll provide a pilot package — free credits to start and a suggested commit if you go Dedicated. I'll include a simple pricing spreadsheet.

[05:42] Marco Alvarez: About logs and PII — we need retention controls and the ability to purge data.
[05:48] Carlos Romero: For hosted we have configurable retention windows and deletion APIs; Private gives you even more control since you can hold logs locally. We'll attach the retention policy doc.

[06:03] Sofia Li: Ok sounds good. Can you show a short run-through of the developer flow?
[06:06] Carlos Romero: Yes. Step 1: sign up and create an API key. Step 2: install SDK or use curl. Step 3: send prompt, get tokens. Step 4: look at token breakdown in console. Step 5: redeem credits in Billing -> Credits. I can drop a one-page quickstart: https://redwood.example.com/quickstart (I'll send actual link in follow-up).

[06:30] Nina Patel: For the quickstart we usually suggest a smoke test: 10 requests at concurrency 2 to see latency, then a small cost calc. You'll tell us the P95 target.

[06:45] Leah Kim: Our P95 target for user-facing requests is 300ms. Is that realistic?
[06:50] Carlos Romero: For short prompts with efficient models yes on hosted you can see sub-200ms for many cases; larger context or heavy generation will push it up. KV cache and prompt engineering helps.

[07:06] Marco Alvarez: You've mentioned "KV cache" a couple times — quick explain?
[07:09] Carlos Romero: KV cache refers to cached key-value pairs for autoregressive models for faster decoding on repeated prefixes — reduces compute and latency for repeated contexts. For many ecom recs it's useful.

[07:28] Sofia Li: Are there restrictions on model versions in hosted? We need a predictable model.
[07:32] Nina Patel: You can pin a model version per route. Redwood's catalog includes verified profiles. For more control Dedicated allows you to pin and hold custom variants longer.

[07:44] Leah Kim: What about rate limits during the pilot? We may need higher limits to test spikes.
[07:48] Carlos Romero: We can temporarily raise limits for pilots after a short verification. We'll coordinate with you.

[08:00] (brief cross talk)
[08:05] Sofia Li: One question from our legal counsel — do you support a DPA and standard security addenda?
[08:09] Nina Patel: Yes, we have a standard DPA and can negotiate addenda as needed. I'll include the DPA PDF in the follow-up.

[08:20] Marco Alvarez: Our timeline — we want to launch a closed beta in 6 weeks and GA in 12. Does that fit with a Redwood pilot?
[08:26] Nina Patel: Yes — the quickstart pilot fits the closed beta timeline. If you need Dedicated for GA we can start sizing based on your beta usage and prepare a Dedicated proposal in parallel.

[08:40] Leah Kim: Are there demo or POC templates?
[08:43] Carlos Romero: We have a POC checklist and a small benchmark harness we can share, plus example Apps that show minimal integration. I'll attach those.

[08:56] Sofia Li: Great. For the quickstart we'll try to measure time-to-first-token and a simple latency and cost snapshot. Is there a recommended way to report results back to you?
[09:03] Nina Patel: A short spreadsheet with sample requests, P95/P50, and token counts is perfect. We'll review and if needed run a joint test.

[09:18] (silence, typing)
[09:22] Marco Alvarez: One gotcha — sometimes request payloads include user PII in metadata. We want to be sure sensitive fields can be redacted.
[09:29] Carlos Romero: We support field-level redaction on ingestion and have data filters; for anything more sensitive Private or Dedicated with customer-managed keys is the path.

[09:42] Leah Kim: Anything else we should be aware of?
[09:45] Nina Patel: For the PLG path: instrument your onboarding funnel to measure time-to-first-successful-generation; that's really the KPI. Also watch for cost surprises on long contexts. We'll give you guidance on truncation and caching.

[10:02] Sofia Li: Ok let's lock next steps.
[10:05] Nina Patel: Recap — I'll send credits + quickstart + security pack + pricing spreadsheet. Carlos will send SDK snippets and a perf harness. You (Verdigris) will run quickstart and return basic metrics. If pilot shows infra limits we schedule a Dedicated/Private deep dive.

[10:25] Leah Kim: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[10:28] Marco Alvarez: Thanks, bye.
[10:30] Carlos Romero: Thanks all.

[10:35] (call ends)

Notes on transcript: occasional transcription errors present; product names sometimes split (e.g., "Red wood"). References provided in chat: https://redwood.example.com/quickstart , https://redwood.example.com/security-pack

End of transcript.
